title: Decoding systemic vascular health and hypertensive disorders in pregnancy through retinal imaging and Visionary AI - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

AbstractHypertensive disorders of pregnancy arise from early placental and systemic vascular dysfunction, yet current first-trimester screening remains imprecise, biologically opaque and logistically challenging. Here we present Visionary AI, an interpretable platform that integrates retinal imaging with graph-based vascular modeling to predict hypertensive disorders before clinical onset. Visionary AI converts retinal images into topological and geometric representations of microvascular structure, enabling risk prediction from biologically grounded vascular features rather than generic image embeddings or clinical variables. In a prospective development cohort of 1,267 pregnancies, Visionary AI achieved strong performance for preeclampsia across population-wide control settings (area under the curve (AUC) = 0.91, average precision (AP) = 0.81). A stability-optimized model transferred without retraining to an independent external validation cohort, achieving AUC = 0.81 and AP = 0.68 and outperforming clinical and deep learning benchmarks. Recurrent features involving retinal vascular topology, geometry, network complexity and hierarchical organization position the maternal retina as a minimally invasive biosensor of systemic vascular health and Visionary AI as a biologically interpretable framework for pregnancy risk stratification.

Hypertensive Disorders Management in Pregnancy

MainHypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDPs), including gestational hypertension (GHTN), preeclampsia, chronic hypertension (CHTN) with superimposed preeclampsia (PEC) and eclampsia, affect 2–15% of pregnancies and represent the second leading cause of maternal mortality worldwide1. HDPs increase the risk of acute maternal complications such as renal dysfunction, pulmonary edema, stroke and death2 and contribute to adverse fetal outcomes, including small for gestational age, preterm delivery and stillbirth3. Long-term, they are associated with elevated maternal risk of hypertension, coronary artery disease, stroke and vascular dementia4,5,6 and elevated offspring risk of cardiovascular and neurodevelopmental disorders7.Despite their burden, HDPs are typically diagnosed after 20 weeks of gestation, when symptoms such as hypertension, proteinuria or organ dysfunction become clinically apparent. Severe features, including systolic blood pressure (BP) ≥ 160 mmHg or diastolic BP ≥ 110 mmHg, thrombocytopenia and visual symptoms, guide early delivery decisions because of high maternal–fetal risk8. Among HDPs, early-onset preeclampsia (EOPE, symptoms appear before 34 weeks) tends to present with more severe complications than late-onset preeclampsia (LOPE). Notably, recent systems biology studies suggest that preeclampsia is not a single disease entity but may reflect multiple distinct biological pathways, with EOPE more frequently associated with placental dysfunction and LOPE more often associated with maternal processes9,10.Mechanistically, preeclampsia is believed to arise, in part, from maternal vascular inflammation and thrombosis that disrupt placental development9,11. Inflammation and thrombosis may impair deep placental invasion12 of the maternal decidua between 10 and 16 weeks of gestation and contribute to later placental injury, including placental atherosis13,14,15,16, a process that shares features with vascular pathology observed in cardiovascular disease. These early deviations from physiologic placentation precede clinical symptoms by weeks or months, underscoring the need for early biomarkers of systemic and placental vascular stress.From a health systems perspective, HDPs accounted for an estimated 2.18 billion USD in US healthcare costs per year (estimated in 2012), largely driven by preterm birth complications17. Their incidence has increased in subsequent years18,19,20 and pregnancies complicated by HDPs typically end approximately 3 weeks earlier than normotensive pregnancies21. Importantly, randomized trials show that early initiation of low-dose aspirin (before 16 weeks) can reduce the risk of preterm delivery with preeclampsia by up to 62%22,23 but this requires early, accurate risk identification.Current diagnostic criteria for preeclampsia rely on late-onset symptoms (hypertension, proteinuria and end-organ dysfunction) that usually manifest in the third trimester24. While known risk factors (for example, prior HDPs, diabetes, obesity and age) provide some predictive value, they lack individual-level accuracy25. The sFlt-1/PlGF ratio is the most validated biomarker but is primarily useful later in pregnancy and in individuals with suspected preeclampsia to aid short-term clinical assessment26. First-trimester screening tools, such as the Fetal Medicine Foundation (FMF) risk calculator27, combine clinical variables with biomarkers or ultrasound but these protocols are expensive, logistically complex and inconsistently implemented28,29. In routine practice, prevention-oriented risk stratification is often reduced to clinical risk factor assessment for aspirin eligibility, which may miss individuals with emerging vascular dysfunction while also identifying broad high-risk groups with limited precision.Increasing evidence suggests a link between placental vascular changes associated with preeclampsia and alterations in the retinal vasculature. Studies of women with established preeclampsia describe retinal signs resembling hypertensive retinopathy, arteriolar narrowing and choroidal changes30,31,32,33,34 and link preeclampsia to increased future risk of retinal diseases35. Further, recent evidence has identified an association between the sFlt-1/PlGF ratio and choroidal thickness as measured by optical coherence tomography (OCT)33,36. A prior postpartum study from our team (31 severe preeclampsia cases and 35 normotensive controls) demonstrated significantly increased median tortuosity in the inferotemporal retinal artery among individuals with preeclampsia37. OCT angiography has revealed that pregnant women who go on to develop placental insufficiency have significantly narrower retinal blood vessels (arterioles and venules) compared to normotensive pregnancies38. These individuals also exhibit reduced capillary density. In separate studies, women with preeclampsia had significantly lower vessel densities in both the superficial and deep capillary plexuses, including in the foveal and parafoveal regions, relative to healthy pregnant or nonpregnant controls39,40. These findings suggest a degree of capillary dropout or ‘vascular rarefaction’ in the retinas of women with preeclampsia. Retinal vessel caliber reduction and reduced perfusion density are consistent with systemic vasoconstriction and endothelial dysfunction, both hallmarks of preeclampsia pathophysiology. Importantly, these changes may be subclinical and may emerge before overt clinical diagnosis, suggesting that the maternal retina could provide a noninvasive window into systemic vascular remodeling during pregnancy.Initial efforts to apply AI to HDP prediction using retinal imaging have been promising but limited. The PROMPT model (preeclampsia risk factor + ophthalmic data + mean arterial pressure prediction test)41 relied heavily on clinical variables (for example, mean arterial pressure) and achieved modest image-only performance using cross-validation at a single site (area under the curve (AUC) = 0.74). Another study combining 45° retinal fundus images with clinical data reported improved accuracy but used a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture that lacks interpretability and biological insight42. Notably, both studies were conducted in homogeneous East Asian populations, further limiting their generalizability and translational impact. Although not originally designed for preeclampsia (or any other pregnancy disorder), RETFound43 is a retinal foundation model that was validated across diverse disease classification tasks. However, direct image-level foundation-model fine-tuning may require larger numbers of outcome events than are typically available in prospective pregnancy cohorts, motivating approaches that reduce image dimensionality while preserving biologically meaningful vascular structure.Here we introduce Visionary AI, an end-to-end computational framework that takes as input retinal images and predicts an individual’s risk of HDPs. Unlike prior approaches that treat retinal images as opaque inputs to generic deep-learning models, Visionary AI models the retinal vasculature as a quantifiable, interpretable biological system—one that may reflect systemic endothelial and angiogenic processes occurring during placental development.We show across a cohort of 1,267 pregnant participants that this framework enables accurate and interpretable prediction of preeclampsia and GHTN months before clinical diagnosis. We further develop a stability-optimized model that reduces complexity and transfers to an independent New York University (NYU) validation cohort without retraining or optimization using NYU outcome labels. By benchmarking Visionary AI against the FMF risk calculator, real-world aspirin-eligibility criteria and RETFound foundation model, we evaluate whether retinal vascular modeling provides information beyond established clinical and image-level deep-learning approaches. Together, these results establish retinal vascular phenotyping as a promising new dimension of pregnancy risk assessment and position Visionary AI as an interpretable, noninvasive framework for detecting early systemic vascular remodeling before HDPs become clinically apparent.ResultsCohort characteristics and study designWe analyzed retinal imaging and clinical data from a Columbia University (CU) development cohort and an independent NYU external validation cohort.The CU cohort included 1,267 pregnant individuals receiving prenatal care at NewYork-Presbyterian/CU Irving Medical Center between 2021 and 2025 (Extended Data Table 1). Within the CU cohort, 55 participants developed preeclampsia (4.3%). One participant with preeclampsia was excluded from retinal image analysis because of poor image quality, yielding 54 preeclampsia cases for retinal-model analyses. Retinal images were acquired during the first, second and third trimesters using the Optos scanning laser ophthalmoscope Primary ultrawidefield imaging system.The independent NYU external validation cohort included 79 pregnant individuals receiving prenatal care at the Mignone Women’s Health Collaborative at NYU Langone Health between 2025 and 2026 (Extended Data Table 2). Within the cohort, 14 participants were diagnosed with preeclampsia during routine prenatal care (17.7%), representing a higher observed prevalence than the annual average prevalence of preeclampsia at NYU Langone Health (~8%). Because predictive values and precision-based metrics are sensitive to outcome prevalence, prevalence-adjusted performance estimates are reported below for both cohorts. One participant with preeclampsia was excluded from retinal image analysis because of poor image quality, yielding 13 preeclampsia cases for retinal-model analyses. NYU images were acquired during the first, second and third trimesters using the Optos California ultrawidefield imaging system.In both cohorts preeclampsia diagnoses were given according to 2013 American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) criteria8 during prenatal care and independently reviewed by maternal–fetal medicine specialists masked to retinal imaging results. Preeclampsia cases were further categorized by severity and timing of onset, including preeclampsia with severe features (SF), preeclampsia without severe features (NSF), EOPE and LOPE; detailed definitions are provided in the Methods. Preeclampsia subtype-specific analyses were treated as descriptive evaluations of model behavior across clinical presentations rather than separately trained subtype-specific models.Extended Data Tables 1 and 2 summarize demographic, clinical and pregnancy-outcome characteristics for the CU and NYU cohorts. Collected variables included maternal age, height, weight, race and ethnicity, tobacco use, obstetric history, preexisting conditions, medication exposures, pregnancy complications and birth outcomes, including small for gestational age, severe small for gestational age, stillbirth, birth weight and Apgar scores.The CU cohort was predominantly Hispanic or Latinx, reflecting the clinical population served at the recruitment site (Supplementary Table 1). Participants who developed preeclampsia were more likely than those who did not to have a history of preeclampsia in a prior pregnancy (16.4% versus 3.8%; P = 4.1 × 10−5, chi-square test) and preexisting hypertension (18.2% versus 3.5%; P = 5.5 × 10−7, chi-square test). Participants who developed GHTN also had higher rates of obesity than normotensive population-wide (PW) controls (65% versus 33%; P = 6.5 × 10−6, chi-square test).The NYU cohort differed from the CU cohort in several clinically relevant respects, including race and ethnicity distribution, older maternal age, higher in vitro fertilization (IVF) prevalence and higher observed preeclampsia prevalence (Supplementary Tables 1 and 2). Among participants with race information available, the NYU cohort included a larger proportion of white and Asian participants than the CU cohort. NYU imaging was also performed using the Optos California ultrawidefield system (CU cohort used the Optos Primary ultrawidefield system) within a different clinical workflow. Together, these demographic, clinical, workflow and imaging-device differences support the use of NYU as a meaningful external validation cohort rather than a near replication of the CU development cohort.The Visionary AI Framework and evaluation strategyVisionary AI is an interpretable retinal vascular modeling framework that uses retinal images to quantify early-pregnancy microvascular structure and predict subsequent HDPs. Figure 1 summarizes the study design and computational workflow, including retinal image acquisition, vessel segmentation, vascular feature extraction and ensemble-based risk prediction.Fig. 1: Study design and Visionary AI computational framework.Full size imagea, Timeline of retinal imaging and clinical outcome ascertainment. Participants were approached for ultrawidefield retinal imaging during the first, second and third trimesters. In the CU development cohort, prediction analyses used first-trimester images when available and second-trimester images only for participants without first-trimester imaging, as specified in the corresponding analyses. The NYU external validation analysis was restricted to retinal images acquired during the first trimester, between 6 and 13 weeks of gestation. Preeclampsia diagnoses were ascertained after 20 weeks of gestation according to clinical criteria. b, Central hypothesis. Retinal vascular structure in early pregnancy contains quantifiable microvascular signatures of systemic vascular dysfunction that precede clinical diagnosis of preeclampsia. c, Visionary AI pipeline. The computational workflow consists of three modules. (i) Image processing: ultrawidefield fundus images are acquired from both eyes, converted into VSIs using a designated AI model and merged when multiple images from the same eye are available to generate a more complete retinal vascular representation. (ii) Feature generation: VSIs are transformed into graph-based, geometric and topological vascular features that quantify complementary aspects of retinal microvascular architecture. (iii) Predictive modeling: semantically grouped vascular feature sets are used to train base learners and their out-of-fold predictions are integrated by a stacked metalearner to generate the final risk prediction.Briefly, retinal images were converted into vessel segmentation images (VSIs) using a dedicated retinal vessel segmentation AI model developed for this study. VSIs provide a binary representation of the retinal vascular tree for downstream feature extraction. When multiple images were available for a given eye, VSIs were merged to generate a more complete vascular representation for analysis. Detailed segmentation model development, image-registration and quality-control procedures are provided in the Methods.Visionary AI then transformed each VSI into biologically interpretable vascular representations. These included graph-based features capturing branching and connectivity, geometric features capturing vessel length, caliber, curvature, angle and tortuosity and higher-order topological features capturing vascular organization and loop structures across scales (Methods and Supplementary Note 1). Together, these feature classes were designed to summarize complementary dimensions of retinal microvascular architecture rather than treat the image as an opaque input to a generic deep-learning classifier.Extracted vascular features were grouped into semantically related feature sets and each feature set was used to train an independent base learner. Base-learner predictions were then integrated through a stacked ensemble framework in which out-of-fold base-learner predictions served as inputs to a metalearner. This architecture allowed the model to combine complementary vascular representations while preserving interpretability at the level of feature classes and retained base learners.Because preeclampsia is a relatively rare outcome, CU model development used leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) to maximize training data while generating held-out predictions for each participant. To reduce the risk of information leakage, base-learner fitting and selection and metalearner training and prediction were implemented within the cross-validation framework, with out-of-fold predictions carried forward between stages, as detailed in the Methods. Model evaluation focused on both internal CU performance and external validation. Within CU, we assessed held-out cross-validated performance and the reproducibility of selected retinal vascular representations across control populations; in parallel, we evaluated model transferability in an independent NYU external validation cohort.Therefore, we evaluated Visionary AI across three increasingly stringent settings. First, a high-contrast analysis tested whether retinal vascular features could distinguish preeclampsia cases from a narrowly defined healthy-control group. Second, a performance-optimized CU model evaluated predictive performance across population-wide control settings within the CU development cohort. Third, to support external validation, a stability-optimized CU model was designed to prioritize reproducibility across nonoverlapping population-wide control groups rather than maximize within-site performance. This stability-optimized model used stability-based hyperparameter selection, minimum-performance and average precision (AP) variability criteria, recursive feature elimination (RFE) and feature-set deduplication to contract the candidate model space before NYU testing. The resulting model was then evaluated on the independent NYU cohort without retraining, refitting or optimization using NYU outcome labels.Retinal vascular features predict preeclampsia across increasingly stringent evaluation settingsHigh-contrast CU analysis identifies preeclampsia-associated retinal vascular signalWe first evaluated Visionary AI in a high-contrast CU analysis to determine whether retinal vascular features captured in early pregnancy contained detectable signals associated with subsequent preeclampsia. In this analysis, preeclampsia cases were compared to a narrowly defined healthy-control group selected to minimize medical, ocular, medication-related and pregnancy-related conditions that could independently influence retinal vascular structure. Healthy controls were drawn from singleton pregnancies without documented preexisting maternal comorbidities, ocular conditions, relevant medication exposures or pregnancy complications; detailed exclusion criteria are provided in the Methods. From 176 eligible healthy controls, 82 were selected to preserve class balance and support approximate matching on key demographic and imaging variables.Visionary AI distinguished participants who later developed preeclampsia from healthy controls with high apparent performance (n = 136, including 54 preeclampsia cases; AUC = 0.94, AP = 0.92, positive predictive value (PPV) = 0.85; Extended Data Fig. 1). We interpret this analysis as an initial proof of signal rather than as the primary estimate of clinical performance, as the comparison was intentionally enriched for phenotypic contrast. Therefore, we subsequently evaluated Visionary AI on broader population-wide CU control settings and on an independent NYU external validation cohort as detailed below.Population-wide CU analyses support preeclampsia prediction in a clinically heterogeneous obstetric populationWe next evaluated whether the retinal vascular signal identified in the high-contrast analysis persisted when preeclampsia cases were compared to broader population-wide controls from the CU cohort. Unlike the selected healthy-control analysis, these population-wide controls were drawn from the larger nonpreeclampsia obstetric population and were intended to better reflect the clinical heterogeneity encountered in prenatal care. We refer to this model as the ‘performance-optimized retinal model’, reflecting its optimization for predictive performance within the CU population-wide evaluation framework.Exclusions from the population-wide control pool were limited to prespecified conditions that could confound the outcome definition or preclude valid retinal-model evaluation, including multifetal gestation, HELLP syndrome, other maternal hypertensive disorders, stillbirth and unavailable or low-quality retinal images (Methods). This design retained participants with common clinical comorbidities, including CHTN, diabetes (gestational and chronic), obesity and fetal outcomes such as growth restriction, thereby providing a more heterogeneous internal evaluation than the healthy-control contrast.Across repeated CU population-wide control samplings, the performance-optimized retinal model maintained strong discriminative performance for preeclampsia, achieving an AUC of 0.91 ± 0.05 and an AP of 0.81 ± 0.11 across sampled control sets (Fig. 2a,b). Because this evaluation used sampled control sets rather than analyzing the full population-wide control pool at once precision–recall (PR) metrics and PPV estimates from these sampled sets should not be interpreted as real-world screening performance at the observed CU preeclampsia prevalence. Therefore, we report threshold-based operating characteristics, including prevalence-adjusted PPV and negative predictive value (NPV), in Extended Data Table 3. LR, logistic regression; RF, random forest; XGB, extreme gradient boosting.Combining Visionary AI with probabilities from the FMF risk calculator27, an established clinical risk prediction tool based on maternal clinical features and pregnancy-related risk factors (Methods), did not materially improve predictive performance relative to Visionary AI alone (AUC = 0.90 ± 0.06, AP = 0.80 ± 0.11). Throughout the retinal-model analyses, we accounted for first pregnancy and prior preeclampsia history as minimal obstetric-history adjustment variables (Methods); however, the primary predictive signal was derived from retinal vascular features rather than from a broader clinical risk model (Fig. 2c). These results suggest that retinal imaging features captured most of the signal relevant to preeclampsia risk in the CU population-wide analysis, with limited incremental contribution from FMF-derived clinical risk information.Because subtype-specific case counts were limited, analyses of SF, NSF, EOPE and LOPE were treated as post hoc stratified evaluations of the same overall preeclampsia model rather than as separately trained subtype-specific classifiers. Visionary AI, trained on all preeclampsia cases, maintained consistent predictive performance across clinical presentations, including SF (n = 38), NSF (n = 16), EOPE (n = 20) and LOPE (n = 34). At an operating point corresponding to a false positive rate (FPR) of 0.08, the true positive rate (TPR) exceeded 0.70 for each subtype (Fig. 2b). To further characterize subtype performance across a range of operating points, Supplementary Tables 3–5 report mean confusion-matrix counts and performance metrics across the ten performance-optimized population-wide control sets at thresholds targeting FPRs of up to 10%, 20% and 30%, respectively. These post hoc analyses suggest that the retinal vascular signal was not restricted to a single preeclampsia presentation, while also underscoring the need for larger cohorts to estimate subtype-specific performance more precisely.A stability-optimized model reduces complexity and prioritizes reproducible retinal vascular signalAlthough the performance-optimized retinal model demonstrated strong predictive performance within CU population-wide analyses, it was designed to maximize internal performance within this population. To further evaluate the robustness of the retinal vascular signal and assess whether predictive performance could be maintained under a more constrained modeling framework, we next developed a stability-optimized model designed to prioritize reproducibility across nonoverlapping population-wide control groups rather than peak performance in any single CU control setting.For the stability-optimized model, we used a control definition that was similar to the performance-optimized population-wide analysis but deliberately more inclusive of the clinical heterogeneity encountered in routine obstetric care. Unlike the performance-optimized model, participants with HDPs other than preeclampsia, including GHTN, were retained in the control pool rather than excluded. Furthermore, in this model, each healthy control was included only once, and the healthy-control group together with the expanded population-wide control pool, including GHTN and CHTN, was divided into five nonoverlapping control settings (Methods). Hyperparameter configurations were selected on the basis of low variability in AP and high minimum AUC across these settings, thereby favoring base learners with consistent performance across control definitions (Supplementary Fig. 1). Candidate base learners that did not meet minimum stability and performance criteria were removed before metalearner training.This stability-based procedure substantially reduced model complexity. The initial search space included 96 candidate base learners, representing 32 retinal vascular feature sets across three model classes. After stability-based hyperparameter selection and RFE, each leave-one-out stability-optimized model retained eight nonredundant base learners per fold. To construct the final model for each population-wide control group, we took the union of base learners selected across leave-one-out folds and retained eight nonredundant learners by prioritizing higher-importance models and removing redundant feature sets (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Methods). Thus, the model used for external validation was intentionally constrained to a small set of reproducible retinal vascular representations rather than optimized solely for maximal internal CU performance.Despite this reduction in model complexity, the stability-optimized model preserved predictive signal in the CU population-wide analyses, supporting the robustness of the selected retinal vascular features (Fig. 3a). Recurrent vascular feature categories and base learners, including graph-based topology, box counting, cumulative size distribution, vessel length or angle and tortuosity-related representations, were repeatedly selected and assigned high importance across population-wide settings (Fig. 3b,c and Supplementary Fig. 2). This consistency across distinct control settings suggests that model performance was driven by stable retinal microvascular representations associated with preeclampsia risk, rather than by control-set-specific patterns, fold-specific model components or unstable feature-selection artifacts.Fig. 3: Stability-optimized Visionary AI predicts preeclampsia in CU population-wide analyses.Full size imagea, ROC and PR curves for the stability-optimized Visionary AI model evaluated in the CU population-wide cohort (n = 1,188; 54 preeclampsia cases). The heat map shows metalearner importance for retained base learners; model classes are indicated in parentheses.The stability-optimized model generalizes to the independent NYU validation cohortWe next evaluated whether the stability-optimized CU model generalized to an independent external validation cohort collected at NYU. This analysis was designed as the primary external test of the retinal vascular signal identified in the CU cohort. The NYU cohort differed from the CU development cohort in institution, population, clinical workflow and ultrawidefield imaging-device configuration and the validation analysis was restricted to retinal images during the first trimester, acquired between 6 and 13 weeks of gestation. The stability-optimized model was evaluated in NYU without retraining, refitting or hyperparameter optimization using NYU outcome labels.Despite these differences in site, population, imaging workflow and clinical setting, Visionary AI maintained robust predictive performance in the independent NYU validation cohort, achieving an AUC of 0.81 and an AP of 0.68 (Fig. 4a). Performance was also preserved in differential-diagnosis analyses distinguishing preeclampsia from other HDPs, including GHTN and CHTN, as well as in subgroup analyses stratified by demographic characteristics, clinical risk factors and quality-control metrics (Extended Data Fig. 3 and Supplementary Figs. 3–5).Fig. 4: Stability-optimized Visionary AI performance predicting preeclampsia on NYU external validation cohort.Full size imagea,b, ROC (left) and PR (right) curves for the stability-optimized model evaluated on the independent NYU external validation cohort (a; n = 66, 13 preeclampsia cases) and ‘the aspirin-recommended subgroup analysis’ (b; n = 33, eight preeclampsia cases). In ROC plots, the diagonal line indicates no-discrimination performance (equivalent to random classification; AUC = 0.5). In PR plots, the horizontal line indicates the expected precision of a random classifier, corresponding to the prevalence of the positive class in the respective evaluation set.Unlike the CU population-wide analyses, the NYU validation did not rely on repeated or balanced sampled control sets. Thus, threshold-based PPV and NPV calculated directly from this cohort reflect the observed preeclampsia prevalence in the NYU validation set. At a stringent operating point, Visionary AI achieved an FPR of 0.02, TPR of 0.46, PPV of 0.86 and NPV of 0.88; at a less stringent operating point, Visionary AI achieved an FPR of 0.13, TPR of 0.69, PPV of 0.56 and NPV of 0.92 (Extended Data Table 4). Because the observed preeclampsia prevalence in the NYU validation cohort was higher than the annual average prevalence at NYU Langone Health (approximately 8%), we additionally report prevalence-adjusted PPV and NPV using the institutional annual prevalence estimate. Under this prevalence-adjusted setting, the stringent operating point corresponded to an estimated PPV of 0.68 and NPV 0.95, whereas the less stringent operating point corresponded to an estimated PPV of 0.31 and NPV of 0.97 (Extended Data Table 4). The preservation of predictive signal in an independent, early-pregnancy validation cohort supports the transferability of the retinal vascular features selected by the stability-optimized CU model.Together, these findings show that the constrained stability-optimized model retained predictive signal beyond the CU development setting. The successful transfer of the stability-optimized model across sites, clinical workflows, populations and imaging-device configurations supports the interpretation that Visionary AI captures reproducible retinal microvascular signatures associated with preeclampsia risk rather than CU-specific control-set artifacts or unstable ensemble behavior.Visionary AI complements established clinical risk-stratification approachesWe next evaluated Visionary AI against established clinical risk-stratification approaches for preeclampsia. To provide a clinically relevant benchmark and avoid potential bias associated with locally trained or modified FMF implementations, we used the official FMF risk calculator portal directly for the independent NYU validation cohort. This analysis used the available maternal demographic, clinical and family-history variables required by the FMF first-trimester risk assessment framework, including maternal age, height, weight, racial origin, CHTN, type 1 diabetes, smoking status, systemic lupus erythematosus, method of conception, obstetric history and family history of preeclampsia (Methods).In the NYU external validation cohort, Visionary AI outperformed FMF across both receiver operating characteristic (ROC) and PR analyses, achieving an AUC of 0.81 and an AP of 0.68, compared to FMF AUC of 0.73 and AP of 0.50 (Fig. 4a). At clinically relevant low-FPR operating points, Visionary AI also achieved higher sensitivity and precision than FMF. At a stringent threshold (FPR of 0.02), Visionary AI achieved a TPR of 0.46 and prevalence-adjusted PPV of 0.68. At a less stringent threshold, Visionary AI achieved an FPR of 0.13, TPR of 0.69 and prevalence-adjusted PPV of 0.31, compared to the FMF FPR of 0.13, TPR of 0.38 and prevalence-adjusted PPV of 0.20 (Extended Data Table 4). Bootstrap resampling of the NYU cohort, stratified by outcome to preserve the observed case prevalence, yielded consistent performance estimates, quantified uncertainty around the ROC, PR and threshold-based metrics and showed that Visionary AI consistently outperformed FMF (Supplementary Table 6).We also compared Visionary AI to the clinical risk-stratification approach used at NYU to guide aspirin eligibility on the basis of ACOG guidelines at approximately 12 weeks of gestation. This benchmark reflects routine prenatal-care decision making on the basis of clinical risk factors, including IVF, maternal age over 35 years and BMI over 30 (Methods). In the NYU cohort, aspirin eligibility identified preeclampsia cases with a TPR of 0.62 but at a substantially higher FPR of 0.47 and lower prevalence-adjusted PPV of 0.1. In contrast, Visionary AI achieved a TPR of 0.69 at a FPR of 0.13 with a prevalence-adjusted PPV of 0.31. These results support the potential of Visionary AI to provide retinal vascular information that is complementary to current clinical risk-factor-based screening and prevention strategies.As an additional sensitivity analysis, we evaluated the stability-optimized Visionary AI model within the subset of NYU participants who were recommended aspirin during pregnancy, a clinically enriched group expected to have elevated baseline risk on the basis of routine obstetric assessment (n = 33, eight preeclampsia cases). In this aspirin-recommended subgroup, Visionary AI maintained strong predictive performance, achieving an AUC of 0.95 and an AP of 0.85, compared to the FMF AUC of 0.76 and AP of 0.65 (Fig. 4b). Combining Visionary AI with FMF probabilities did not improve performance (AUC = 0.78, AP = 0.67), consistent with the broader analysis. Although this subgroup analysis is limited by sample size, the preservation of strong retinal-model performance among aspirin-recommended individuals suggests that Visionary AI captures retinal vascular information not fully represented by the clinical risk factors used to guide aspirin recommendation.Because the CU cohort lacked some FMF variables, including family history of preeclampsia and a direct systemic lupus erythematosus variable, CU FMF comparisons were treated as secondary benchmarking analyses and interpreted with caution. Across both CU performance-optimized and stability-optimized analyses, Visionary AI showed stronger performance than FMF-derived clinical risk estimates; however, the NYU analysis represents the most complete and clinically relevant FMF comparison in the revised manuscript. Both baselines were trained on the CU development cohort using participant-level LOOCV. By quantifying early retinal microvascular patterns associated with later diagnosed preeclampsia and related hypertensive disorders, Visionary AI offers a biologically grounded, interpretable and scalable framework for early risk stratification across diverse obstetric populations.A central advance of this work is the use of graph-based retinal vascular modeling to capture microvascular organization, including topology, vessel geometry, network complexity and hierarchical structure. These representations were predictive in the development cohort and transferred to an independent validation cohort without retraining or optimization using outcome labels. This cross-cohort transfer is particularly important, as the two cohorts differed in population, clinical workflow and imaging-device configuration, providing an initial test of robustness across real-world sources of variation.Another key advance of Visionary AI is its interpretable framework. The retinal features identified by Visionary AI are biologically plausible in the context of preeclampsia and related hypertensive disorders. Preeclampsia is characterized by systemic endothelial dysfunction, altered vascular tone, antiangiogenic signaling and microvascular injury. The retinal signatures detected here, involving altered vascular topology, branching structure, tortuosity, vessel caliber, loop organization and asymmetry, are consistent with early vascular simplification and reduced network resilience.These retinal signatures mirror vascular patterns reported in established preeclampsia and other hypertensive states40,45, including reduced vessel density, lower perfusion, diminished branching complexity and increased vascular asymmetry. Because these analyses are based on predictive feature attribution and univariate associations, they should be interpreted as hypothesis generating rather than causal evidence.Visionary AI captures early signs of vascular simplification, a hallmark of preeclampsia, consistent with two complementary pathological processes: capillary network rarefaction40,45 (loss of small vessels, reduced density and impaired branching complexity) and arteriolar wall thickening (hypertrophic remodeling that narrows luminal diameter and increases resistance)46. These processes jointly contribute to reduced network redundancy, lower perfusion and heightened susceptibility to ischemic injury12,14,47. Our topological metrics, including changes in loop structure, asymmetry and branching organization, are consistent with early deviations in vascular organization and network resilience. Inferior retinal differences in feature importance further align with known variations in regional blood flow48. The fact that Visionary AI identifies these shifts early in gestation underscores the system-wide vascular impairment characteristic of HDPs and provides potential mechanistic insight into disease pathways.We benchmarked Visionary AI against established clinical risk-stratification approaches and direct image-level deep-learning methods. In the NYU external validation cohort, Visionary AI outperformed the official FMF risk calculator, an established clinical risk prediction tool based on maternal clinical features and pregnancy-related risk factors. We also compared Visionary AI to the clinical risk-stratification approach used at NYU to guide aspirin eligibility at approximately 12 weeks of gestation. This comparison is clinically important because aspirin eligibility reflects the current prevention-oriented workflow; individuals identified as higher risk on the basis of routine obstetric risk factors are recommended low-dose aspirin. Visionary AI achieved higher sensitivity and precision at lower FPRs than aspirin eligibility alone, suggesting that retinal vascular features capture risk information not fully represented by standard clinical criteria. In an additional aspirin-recommended subgroup, Visionary AI maintained strong performance despite enrichment for individuals already identified as higher risk by routine clinical assessment, further supporting its potential to refine risk stratification within clinically high-risk groups. Together, these analyses suggest that Visionary AI provides complementary retinal microvascular information beyond both FMF-based risk estimation and ACOG-recommended aspirin-eligibility criteria.We also compared Visionary AI to two deep-learning models: RETFound, a retinal foundation model, and Inception-ResNet-v2, a CNN. Both deep-learning approaches performed near chance on the CU development cohort and the independent NYU validation cohort, whereas Visionary AI had strong performance and preserved predictive signal on the external validation cohort. This comparison should be interpreted cautiously, because end-to-end deep-learning models may require substantially larger numbers of outcome events for effective task-specific fine-tuning. Nevertheless, these results support the rationale for Visionary AI’s feature-based design; by converting retinal images into biologically meaningful vascular graph topology, geometry, nesting-tree and organization features, Visionary AI reduces the dimensionality of the prediction problem and may be better suited to limited-event pregnancy cohorts than direct image-level fine-tuning.Visionary AI offers a fast, noninvasive and cost-effective screening strategy suitable for both high-resource and low-resource settings. Retinal fundus imaging requires no laboratory infrastructure, takes less than 2 min to perform and can be operated by nonspecialists. As our computational pipeline is automated and does not require manual image grading, it eliminates subjectivity and reduces implementation barriers. Visionary AI may provide value as a retinal microvascular adjunct to existing obstetric risk assessment by capturing biological information not fully represented by clinical risk factors, FMF-based prediction or aspirin-eligibility criteria. In practice, this could support earlier and more refined risk stratification, including identification of individuals who may benefit from intensified surveillance, preventive interventions or referral pathways. Additional prospective studies will be needed to determine whether Visionary AI is best deployed as a standalone screening tool, as part of a multimodal model with established clinical and biomarker-based approaches or as a second-line test to refine risk among individuals already classified as clinically high risk. These studies will also be essential to define calibration, optimal operating thresholds, clinical utility, workflow integration and feasibility across diverse healthcare settings.Several limitations warrant consideration. Although our prospective CU development cohort was large for imaging-based pregnancy research, the absolute number of preeclampsia cases was modest because of low baseline prevalence. The addition of the NYU cohort provides independent external validation across site, population, clinical workflow and imaging-device configuration; however, the validation cohort remains modest in size and has a higher observed preeclampsia prevalence than the annual institutional average. Therefore, we report prevalence-adjusted PPV and NPV but larger prospective validation cohorts will be needed to estimate screening performance, calibration and decision thresholds more precisely across different baseline-risk settings.Additional limitations include the relatively small number of cases available for subtype-specific analyses, including EOPE and NSF. These analyses were, therefore, treated as post hoc stratified evaluations of a model trained on overall preeclampsia rather than independently trained subtype-specific classifiers. Although the stability-optimized model reduced complexity and transferred to NYU without retraining, the current study remains limited to two US academic medical centers. Importantly, the CU and NYU cohorts already differed in imaging device, acquisition workflow, race and ethnicity distribution and comorbidity profiles, providing an initial test of robustness across these sources of variation. Future studies should extend this validation to larger and more geographically diverse populations, additional healthcare systems, broader baseline-risk settings and lower-cost retinal imaging devices to determine how well the retinal vascular signal transfers across implementation contexts.Future and ongoing work includes multisite international validation and integration with circulating biomarkers and placental pathology for deeper mechanistic insight. Together, these efforts will determine how Visionary AI can be integrated into early pregnancy care to improve risk stratification and reduce the burden of HDPs.MethodsStudy design, ethics and participantsThis prospective study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards of CU and NYU and adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki. Data availability

Because of participant privacy protections, the sensitive nature of retinal imaging and linked clinical pregnancy data and the terms of study consent and institutional review board approvals, individual-level data cannot be deposited in a public repository. Summary-level data supporting the key findings are included in the main text and Supplementary Information. Deidentified participant-level analysis datasets supporting the findings of this study, including derived retinal vascular features, outcome labels, relevant clinical covariates and accompanying metadata/data dictionaries, will be made available to qualified investigators upon reasonable request. Access will be contingent on approval by the relevant institutional review boards, confirmation that the proposed use is consistent with participant consent and applicable regulatory requirements and execution of an appropriate data use agreement. Data will be provided for noncommercial research purposes related to replication, validation or extension of the reported findings. Requests should be sent to Liat.Shenhav@nyulangone.org.
